items.title: Equality Act 2010, section 19: Indirect discrimination
items.why: The effect-based test an algorithmic rule is judged by. Note s.19(3) lists eight characteristics: pregnancy and maternity is not among them.
items.quote: A applies to B a provision, criterion or practice which is discriminatory in relation to a relevant protected characteristic of B's

items.title: Equality Act 2010, section 109: Liability of employers and principals
items.why: Acts of an agent with authority are treated as the principal's, whatever the principal knew. The reasonable-steps defence in (4) covers employees only.
items.quote: It does not matter whether that thing is done with the employer's or principal's knowledge or approval.

items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: What about fairness, bias and discrimination?
items.locator: Sections 'Why might an AI system lead to discrimination?' and 'Should we just remove all sensitive data?'
items.why: Source of the quotation on proxy variables. Under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025; covers data protection only, not the Equality Act.
items.quote: enable the model to reproduce patterns of discrimination associated with those characteristics, even if the designers did not intend this

items.title: AI tools in recruitment: audit outcomes report
items.why: Source of the figure (296 recommendations, p.12; all accepted, p.4). Records tools that let recruiters filter by protected characteristics and that inferred gender and ethnicity from names (p.3).
items.quote: to understand how the development and provision of AI recruitment tools complies with UK data protection law

items.title: Responsible AI in Recruitment
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Sections on assurance mechanisms before procurement and before deployment
items.why: Supports 'consulted before purchase or deployment'; gives employment gaps as a worked example of a proxy.
items.quote: A process to anticipate the wider effects of a system/product on environmental, equality, human rights, data protection, or other outcomes.

items.title: AI and biometrics strategy
items.why: Names recruitment and public services as the focus for automated decision-making. Does not name credit.
items.quote: focusing on how they are used in recruitment and in public services

items.title: Equality Act 2010, section 4: The protected characteristics
items.quote: The following characteristics are protected characteristics
items.why: The statutory list any mapping has to cover: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, sexual orientation. Extent shown as England, Wales and Scotland. The page lists amendments by a 2025 Act not yet applied to other sections of the Act; none alters this list.

items.title: Equality Act 2010, section 13: Direct discrimination
items.quote: A person (A) discriminates against another (B) if, because of a protected characteristic, A treats B less favourably than A treats or would treat others.
items.why: The second route to liability beside indirect discrimination. Direct discrimination cannot be justified, except for age (s.13(2)), so a system that uses a protected characteristic, or a near-perfect stand-in for one, carries more exposure than one with a disparate effect. The section says nothing about algorithms; how it applies to proxies has not been settled by a UK court.

items.title: Equality Act 2010, section 29: Provision of services, etc.
items.quote: must not discriminate against a person requiring the service by not providing the person with the service
items.why: Carries the duty beyond employment to anyone providing a service to the public, paid or not, and to the exercise of public functions (s.29(6)). The legal basis for saying that pricing, lending and service triage carry the same exposure as recruitment. Exceptions elsewhere in the Act (for example for insurance and age) were not read in this pass.

items.title: Equality Act 2010, section 149: Public sector equality duty
items.quote: remove or minimise disadvantages suffered by persons who share a relevant protected characteristic that are connected to that characteristic
items.why: For public authorities, and others exercising public functions, the duty to have due regard to equality before and while a policy is adopted. This is the duty the Court of Appeal applied to facial recognition software in Bridges. It binds public functions only; a private firm has no equivalent general duty. Marriage and civil partnership is not a relevant characteristic for this duty (s.149(7)).

items.title: R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2020] EWCA Civ 1058
items.publisher: Court of Appeal (Civil Division), published by The National Archives (Find Case Law)
items.quote: It requires the taking of reasonable steps to make enquiries about what may not yet be known to a public authority about the potential impact
items.why: The leading UK judgment on equality duties and an AI system. The court held that the public sector equality duty requires reasonable enquiry into what is not yet known about a system's effect on people of different race and sex, before and during use, and that the duty cannot be delegated to a supplier. Public authorities only; the court made no finding that the software was in fact biased (para 182).

items.title: Review into bias in algorithmic decision-making
items.publisher: Centre for Data Ethics and Innovation
items.locator: Executive summary, 'Guidance to organisation leaders and boards'; section 2.4 on proxies and direct discrimination
items.quote: Understanding their legal obligations and having carried out appropriate impact assessments
items.why: The government-commissioned review of recruitment, financial services, policing and local government. It tells boards to put named leaders in place who are accountable for understanding the tools, their legal obligations and impact assessments, which is the substance of this criterion. Advisory, not binding; dated 2020, so it predates the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 and the current rules on automated decisions.

items.title: Algorithms: How they can reduce competition and harm consumers
items.quote: even simple policies implementing regional pricing or varying services available in different areas could potentially result in indirect discrimination
items.why: A regulator outside data protection saying that pricing and service algorithms, not only recruitment tools, can discriminate, because people with protected characteristics are unevenly spread by area. Supports mapping consumer-facing uses. A research paper setting out the regulator's thinking, not guidance or a finding against any firm; its examples come from published studies, several of them from the United States.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government
items.locator: 'Using AI safely and responsibly', Ethics: Fairness, bias and discrimination, practical recommendations
items.quote: difficulties with making links between abstract algorithmic groupings and protected groups
items.why: Current government guidance. It warns that AI can make Equality Act duties harder to meet because a model's groupings do not line up with protected groups, and that bias compounds when characteristics combine: two reasons a mapping has to be deliberate. Written for government departments and public bodies; guidance, not law, for anyone else.

items.title: EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), Article 27: Fundamental rights impact assessment for high-risk AI systems
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected by its use in the specific context
items.why: The nearest thing in binding law to a required map: before first use, certain deployers of high-risk systems must record which groups of people are likely to be affected and the specific risks of harm to them. The Commission's copy of the consolidated text as at 27 July 2026. EU law: it reaches UK firms only where they deploy in the EU; it covers public bodies, private providers of public services, and credit scoring and life and health insurance pricing, not every deployer. Application dates were moved by the Digital Omnibus and are not stated here.

items.title: Tax Administration fined for discriminatory and unlawful data processing
items.quote: it used applicants' nationality (Dutch/not Dutch) as an indicator in a system that automatically designated certain applications as risky
items.why: The regulator's enforcement decision in the Dutch childcare benefits affair: a EUR 2.75 million fine for using nationality as a risk indicator in an automated system. What an unmapped characteristic in a risk model looks like when it reaches a regulator. Netherlands, under the EU GDPR, not the Equality Act; this is the regulator's English notice, and the decision itself (in Dutch) was not read.

items.title: Discrimination in the Age of Algorithms (NBER Working Paper 25548)
items.publisher: Jon Kleinberg, Jens Ludwig, Sendhil Mullainathan and Cass R. Sunstein; National Bureau of Economic Research
items.quote: with appropriate requirements in place, the use of algorithms will make it possible to more easily examine and interrogate the entire decision process
items.why: Argues that algorithms can make discrimination easier to detect than human decisions, but only if the organisation keeps the records that allow examination. The case for mapping and documenting rather than avoiding the question. Working-paper version of an article in the Journal of Legal Analysis (vol. 10, 2018); legal analysis under United States law, not an empirical study.

items.title: Why Fairness Cannot Be Automated: Bridging the Gap Between EU Non-Discrimination Law and AI
items.publisher: Sandra Wachter, Brent Mittelstadt and Chris Russell (arXiv preprint)
items.quote: we show how the legal protection offered by non-discrimination law is challenged when AI, not humans, discriminate
items.why: Explains why algorithmic discrimination goes unnoticed: human prejudice gives victims a signal that something is wrong, an algorithm does not. So the organisation cannot rely on complaints to tell it where its exposure lies. Preprint (arXiv, linked to an SSRN paper); the journal version was not read. It analyses EU non-discrimination law and Court of Justice case law, not the Equality Act 2010.

items.title: Protected Grounds and the System of Non-Discrimination Law in the Context of Algorithmic Decision-Making and Artificial Intelligence
items.publisher: Janneke Gerards and Frederik Zuiderveen Borgesius (arXiv; Colorado Technology Law Journal, 2022)
items.quote: algorithms can generate new categories of people based on seemingly innocuous characteristics, such as web browser preference or apartment number
items.why: A limit on any map drawn only against the listed characteristics. The authors show that algorithms sort people into new groups that match no protected ground, so the differentiation can escape discrimination law and still be unfair. A reason to record what a system actually differentiates on, not only the nine characteristics. Law-journal article (2022), authors' copy posted to arXiv in 2025; European law, not the Equality Act. Only the abstract was read.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (US)
items.locator: Table 2, MAP 5 and MAP 5.1 (p. 27); section 3.7, 'Fair - with Harmful Bias Managed' (p. 17)
items.quote: Impacts to individuals, groups, communities, organizations, and society are characterized.
items.why: International comparator. The most widely used voluntary AI risk framework makes mapping impacts on groups a named outcome (MAP 5) and treats managing harmful bias as a property of a trustworthy system. Voluntary; United States; written without reference to UK equality law.
